newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court convicts E.German spymaster Wolf.
newsitem.headline: German court convicts E.German spymaster Wolf.

text.p: A German court convicted legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf on Tuesday of kidnapping, coercion and bodily harm for Cold War crimes that could have spilled from the pages of a spy thriller.

Wolf, who ran one of the world's most feared foreign intellience agencies for more than 30 years, walked free after he was handed a two-year suspended sentence for supervising three violent snatches his agents made during the 1950s and 1960s.
The tall, bespectacled Wolf was also ordered to pay a 50,000 mark fine to a children's orphanage on top of the unspecified court costs incurred during the six-month long trial.

A frown flashed across Wolf's well-tanned face when judge Ina Obst-Oellers read the verdict in a windowless basement courtroom packed with more than 80 journalists and Wolf well-wishers, many of whom had applauded when he entered.
Wolf gazed silently with an icy stare for nearly two hours as the judge detailed the three Cold War kidnappings that she said he had ordered.

"This was a political trial," Wolf said afterwards. "Every agent in both East and West could be prosecuted for kidnapping. The charges were a pretext in order to reach a political judgement. As a result I cannot recognise the ruling."
"I do not agree with the legal position of this court," Wolf said. "During the Cold War I did what I did for my country."

Wolf had been found guilty of treason in 1993 by the same Duesseldorf court. But that ruling was overturned by the supreme court in 1995 because it ruled he could not be convicted for spying from East Berlin on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.

Federal prosecutor Joachim Lampe appeared relieved that Wolf had now been convicted for crimes that were also against East German law. Prosecutors had painstakingly collected evidence on the three cases from 1955 to 1963.
"There was no alternative to putting him on trial," said Lampe in claiming a victory. "The ruling today refutes the theory that this was a political trial."

Impeccably dressed in a dapper gray suit, the fit-looking Wolf appeared decades younger than his 74 years. He could have easily been mistaken for a corporate chief executive rather than one of the world's most successful spies.

After the lengthy judgement was read, Wolf quietly kissed his wife on the cheek. He slipped out of a side entrance with his two attorneys before later stepping in front of scores of television cameras and journalists.
"I suppose I should be able to live with this," Wolf said, noting that prosecutors had sought a jail term of three-and-a-half years in this trial and seven years in prison in his first trial.

Wolf was long an elusive figure who ran a network of around 4,000 foreign-based agents from his East Berlin headquarters. He was dubbed "the man without a face" by his admiring Western counterparters, who for decades had no idea what he looked like.
Thriller writers often used him as a model when depicting a sinister communist spy chief. The three Cold War cases used to prosecute Wolf could have figured in any respectable spy novel.

In 1955, a West Berlin woman named Christa Trapp who worked for the U.S. High Commission was abducted in West Berlin with her mother and taken to East Berlin. She was told she would never see her mother again unless she promised to spy for Wolf.
Trapp reluctantly agreed, but reported the incident upon her her return to West Berlin the next day. Shaken by the ordeal, she soon emigrated to the United States.
In 1962, an East German spy and his girlfriend who defected to the West were captured in Austria and beaten unconcious. They were spirited back to East Germany and spent long terms in jail.

And in 1959 an East German typesetter named Georg Angerer was held by Wolf's agents for six months in an ultimately unsuccessful bid to force Angerer to sign defamatory statements about Chancellor Willy Brandt, mayor of West Berlin at the time, whom he had known during their wartime exile in Norway.
